text: Service level management exists to set clear, business-based targets for service levels, and to ensure delivery is properly assessed, monitored, and managed against those targets. Two things matter equally there: targets written in terms the business cares about, and someone actually watching performance after the agreement is signed.

Three related agreements show up constantly, and mixing them up is a common mistake. An SLA is the agreement between provider and customer — the business-facing promise, like 99.5% availability during business hours. An OLA is internal, between teams in the same provider organization that have to cooperate to hit that SLA.

An underpinning contract is external — a formal contract with a third-party supplier, like an internet provider or SaaS vendor, whose performance feeds into whether the SLA can be met at all. The SLA is the promise; the OLA and underpinning contract are what has to hold up for that promise to be kept.

A purely technical SLA might promise 99.9% server uptime — true, while the business still has a terrible experience because a slow network link or broken integration makes the order system unusable anyway. ITIL 4 pushes toward output-based SLAs instead: targets written in terms of the outcome the business actually experiences.

Component metrics like server uptime or network latency still get monitored — they're useful for diagnosing where a problem lives — but they support the output-based target rather than replacing it as what gets reported to the business.

Signing the SLA is day one, not the deliverable. The real work is continuous monitoring, regular service reviews with the customer, and renegotiating targets when they turn out unrealistic. Next up: the service desk, the single point of contact behind all of this.
